column2: But if he does otherwise, Yudhishthira, out of desire, then he is, as before seen, a brahmana-Chandala.
A son equal to the brahmin wife's and one born of the kshatriya wife, king, have no distinction here between the two classes.

But in the world a kshatriya woman is never equal in birth to a brahmin woman; the brahmin wife's first son should be greater, best of kings; the greater too takes more from the father's wealth, Yudhishthira.
As a kshatriya woman is never equal to a brahmin woman, so a vaishya woman is never equal to a kshatriya woman.
Prosperity, kingdom and treasury are seen ordained for kshatriyas, Yudhishthira, and the earth to the ocean's edge.
A kshatriya by his own dharma gains greater prosperity; a king is the bearer of the rod; protection is from none but a kshatriya.
Brahmanas are greatly fortunate, gods even of the gods; towards them a king should behave with honour by rule.
Knowing the eternal, imperishable dharma set forth by sages, a kshatriya protects the people, who are being lost to their own dharma.
When wealth and wives are being carried off by robbers on all sides, the king is the saviour of all classes.
The kshatriya woman's son should be greater than the vaishya woman's son, without doubt; he should take more from his father's wealth, Yudhishthira.
[Yudhishthira said:] Grandfather, you have told rightly, king, of the brahmana's property; how would the regulation be for the other classes?
[Bhishma said:] For a kshatriya too two wives are ordained, descendant of the Kurus, and a third may be a shudra, but not as an example.
This is the order for kshatriyas, Yudhishthira; a kshatriya's property should be made eightfold, Yudhishthira.
The son of the kshatriya wife should take four shares of the father's wealth; and what is the father's war spoil, he may take it.
The vaishya wife's son gets three shares, and the shudra wife's son the eighth; he too may take what the father gave, and cannot take what is not given.
A vaishya has only one wife, descendant of the Kurus, or a second may be a shudra, but not as an example.
For a vaishya living with a vaishya wife and a shudra wife, bull of the Bharatas, the regulation between them is remembered.
A vaishya's property should be made fivefold, bull of the Bharatas; I shall tell the division among their offspring, lord of men.
Four shares of the father's wealth are to be taken by the vaishya wife's son, and the fifth share, Bharata, for the shudra wife's son.
He too may take what the father gave and cannot take what is not given; one born of the three classes of a shudra is one to be given wealth.
A shudra should have only a wife of his own class, never another; a shudra's share should be equal even if he has a hundred sons.
Among sons born of wives of the same class, without distinction, equal shares in wealth are remembered for all classes.
The eldest's share is the eldest, one portion of the chief; this rule of inheritance, Partha, was told before by the Self-born.
Among those born of wives of the same class there is no other distinction, king; the earlier one is distinguished by the earlier marriage.
The eldest should take the one chief portion, and be equal among sons also; the middle takes the middle, and the youngest the youngest.
Thus among all the classes the same-class ones gain excellence; the great sage Marichi's son Kashyapa also said this.
[Yudhishthira said:] For those born by mixture of classes by this rule, what dharma and what deeds are theirs? Tell me, grandfather.
[Bhishma said:] The Prajapati created the deeds of the four classes and the fourfold order alone first, for sacrifice.
Of four wives of a brahmana, his self is born of two; those of two lower, in order, are born of their mother's class.
The son of a shudra woman is a better kind of dog to a brahmana; they call him Parashava; he should be the servant of his own family and never leave his own conduct.
Having considered all means, he should uphold the thread of his own family; whether eldest or youngest, a son of a twice-born should be obedient and given to giving.
Of three wives of kshatriya rank, his self is born of two; in the third, of lower class, a shudra, called Ugra, is remembered.
Of a vaishya's two wives, his self is born of two; a shudra woman and one for a shudra produces a shudra only.
From this, one better but worse, who violates the teacher's wife, begets an outcaste class, reviled in the fourfold order.
A bandi is born from a vaishya, a Magadha living by speech; from a shudra, a Nishada, fish-killer, by the transgression with a kshatriya woman.
From a shudra by a vaishya woman is born an Ayogava, of village dharma; he cannot be received by brahmanas, a carpenter, living in the forest.
These too beget their own class in their own wombs; in their mother's class are born the best of the lowest wombs.
As in the four classes his self is born of two, so those born in immediate succession are chiefly outcastes.
These too beget their own class in their own wombs; living with one another they produce the despised.
As a shudra with a brahmin woman begets an outcaste creature, so an outcaste from one more outcaste beget from the fourfold order.
Living in reverse order, from the outcaste a more outcaste again; the lower are born from the lower; those classes are only fifteen.
By going to the unapproachable, mixture of classes occurs; among the Vratyas Sairandhras are born, and among the Magadhas one who knows adornment and service, not a slave, living as a slave.
From him an Ayogava begets a hunter living in the forest, and a Vaidehaka begets a Maireyaka and a Madhuka.
A Nishada begets a Mudgara, and a Dasha who lives by boats; a Chandala begets a Mritapa and the very despised Shvapaka.
A Magadhi begets four fierce ones living by deceit: a cook who makes meat tasty, called Saugandha.
From a Vaidehaka a most sinful, cruel one living by his wife; from a Nishada a Madranabha who travels by donkey-cart.
From a Chandala a Pulkasa, eating donkey, horse and elephant, wearing the clothes of the dead, eating from broken vessels.
Those three are born of Ayogava women of lower class: from a Vaidehaka a low one, Andhra, living outside the village.
A Karavara is born of a Nishadi; from a leatherworker; and from a Chandala a Pandusopaka dealing in skins.
An Ahindika is born of a Nishada by a Vaidehi woman; by a Chandala a Sopaka living like a Mudgara.
A Nishadi by a Chandala has a son, an Antavasayin; a Suta moving in cremation grounds, outcast even by outcastes.
Thus these castes in mixture, from transgression of father and mother, hidden or manifest, are to be known by their own deeds.
The dharma is of the four classes alone; there is none for another; among those devoid of dharma no one here has a name.
By those who came by chance, excluded from sacrifice, outcastes are born of outcastes according to livelihood and refuge.
They use crossroads, cremation grounds, mountains, other trees, ornaments and implements.
They give help for cows and brahmanas, without doubt; non-cruelty, compassion, truthful speech, and forgiveness,
and protection with their own bodies bring success to outcastes; there, tiger among men, I have no doubt.
A wise man should beget in the classes as told by instruction, for a son of low womb would sink him as a stone sinks one wishing to cross water.
Women lead astray in the world the ignorant or even the learned, who follow desire and anger.
The nature of women is a fault of men here; therefore the wise do not become attached to women.
[Yudhishthira said:] A man outside the classes, unknown, born of a stained womb, like a noble, how can we know him, king?
[Bhishma said:] One born of a stained womb, joined with various conduct, by deeds practised by the good, the purity of his womb is to be known.
Ignobleness, bad conduct, cruelty and inactivity reveal here in the world a man born of a stained womb.
He takes either his father's conduct or his mother's or both; a mixed man never restrains his own nature.
As a tiger similar in form to his mother and father is born spotted, so a man restrains his own womb.
When the stream of the family is covered, he whose womb is mixed takes up that conduct, little or much.
One who moves on an artificial path with noble form and conduct is ruled in his resolve by his own nature, whether of his own class or another.
Among beings of various conduct and various occupations in the world, birth equal to conduct is well joined and does not turn away.
Here a man's body is drawn by sattva; sattva is eldest, middle and youngest; one delights in equal sattva.
One should not honour even a more senior man if devoid of conduct; but one should honour even a shudra of good conduct who knows dharma.
A man declares himself by his deeds, good and bad, made by his own conduct and character; and a man makes even his lost family bright again by his deeds.
Among all these wombs and the other mixed ones, a wise man should avoid those in which he would not beget himself.
[Yudhishthira said:] Many disputes are heard about sons; for us who are bewildered you ought to cut the doubt, king.
[Bhishma said:] The son of oneself is to be known, and the one born immediately after, the appointed-born, the one born of a sister's line,
the son of a fallen man's wife united with the husband, two given and made, and another, one of the taken-up.
The six born of degradation and the born of a lower class, and the born of an unmarried girl: these have been told; know them, Bharata.
[Yudhishthira said:] Who are the six born of degradation, and who are the lower-born? You ought to explain all this truly.
[Bhishma said:] The sons born to a brahmana in the three classes, Yudhishthira, and those of two classes to a kshatriya, Bharata,
one of two classes, and here indicated: they are the six born of degradation; hear also the lower-born.
A Chandala, a Vratya, and a Vena born of a brahmin woman, kshatriya woman, and vaishya woman to a shudra: these three are seen as lower-born.
[Yudhishthira said:] Some say the field-born son, some the seed-born; to whom do these two sons belong? Tell me, grandfather.
[Bhishma said:] A son may be of the seed, or abandoned, or field-born, or taken-up having broken an agreement; learn this from me.
[Yudhishthira said:] We know the seed-born son; how is the field-born's origin? And how do we know the taken-up son, having left the agreement?
[Bhishma said:] One who, having begotten a son of himself, abandons him for another cause: the seed is no reason there; he would belong to the field's owner.
A man wishing a son, for a son's sake, chooses a woman, lord of men; there the field is the standard, and the son is not self-born.
Elsewhere a field-born son is seen, bull of the Bharatas; the self cannot be killed, for he has attained the example.
Some made son is seen by adoption; neither seed nor field is the standard there, Yudhishthira.
[Yudhishthira said:] What kind of made son is seen by adoption, where neither seed, field nor standard is observed, Bharata?
[Bhishma said:] One who is seen on the road abandoned by mother and father, whose mother and father are not known, he is the made son.
In whom one sees lordship over one without a lord, he of his own class should support him, and he is born of his own class.
[Yudhishthira said:] How should his rite be applied, and to whom? How should a maiden be given? Tell me that, grandfather.
[Bhishma said:] One should do his rite as for oneself, and as a master.
One abandoned by mother and father who takes to his own class, unfallen one, one should perform his rite by his gotra and class.
Then a maiden is to be given by his class, Yudhishthira; and to perform the rite, by the mother's gotra, in the determination of mother's class.
The Kanina and Adhyudha-born are to be known as sons of fault; they are both to be given rites as if their own sons: so it is settled.
Field-born, lower-born and those taken up should have rites applied by brahmanas and the rest as to themselves.
This is seen as the determination of the classes in the law books. All this has been told to you; what more do you wish to hear?
[Bhishma said:] Come, I shall tell you an ancient event, greatly radiant one: the conversation of Nahusha and the great sage Chyavana.
Long ago the great sage Chyavana Bhargava, bull of the Bharatas, of great vows, began a water-dwelling vow.
Having killed pride, anger, joy and grief, the sage, firm in his vow, stayed twelve years living in water.
He placed supreme, good trust in all beings, among creatures living in water, like the cool-rayed moon.
Becoming still and pure, and bowing to the gods, he entered the water between the Ganga and the Yamuna.
He took on his head the very terrible, terrible-sounding force of the Ganga and Yamuna, swift as the wind.
The Ganga and Yamuna and the rivers following them circled the sage and did not trouble him.
The great sage slept in the water, like a log, and then the wise one stood upright, bull of the Bharatas.
Then once, at some time, men who lived by fishing came to that place with nets in hand, greatly radiant one.
Many Nishadas there, bent on taking fish, exerting, strong, brave, never turning back from the waters, came to that place, resolved on net-work.
They set the net with special care, lord of men, having reached the fish water, best of the Bharatas.
Then those fishermen, wishing fish, by many means cast it into the waters of the Ganga and Yamuna with nets.
Their net, well spread and newly made, was of suitable width and length for the water.
Then all of them, scattering a very large, strong, well-twisted net on every side, dragged it.
Fearless and glad, controlled by one another, they caught fish and other water-creatures there.
So by the net, by chance, they dragged along Chyavana, Bhrigu's descendant, surrounded by fish, great king.
His limbs smeared with river weeds, with green beard and matted hair, covered with clinging shells in his limbs and bellies, as if painted,
seeing him drawn up by the net, that knower of the Vedas, the fishermen with joined palms fell on the ground with their heads.
From distress and fear, and from dragging the net, and from being dragged on land, the fish perished.
Seeing that slaughter of fish, the sage was filled with pity and sighed again and again.
[The Nishadas said:] "Show us favour in the sin done through ignorance; tell us what dear thing we may do for you, great sage."
[Bhishma said:] Thus addressed, Chyavana, standing amid the fish, said: "Hear with attention the highest wish I have today.
I shall go with the fish, giving up breath or by sale; I cannot leave these who have lived with me in the water."
Thus addressed, the Nishadas, trembling with great fear, all with downcast faces, told Nahusha.
Having done purification as is right, the king, with joined palms and controlled, announced himself to the great-souled Chyavana.
And the king's priest honoured him, truthful of vow, greatly fortunate, god-like, lord of men.
[Nahusha said:] "What dear thing shall I do for you? You ought to tell me; I shall do all, blessed one, even if very hard."
[Chyavana said:] "These fishermen, who live by fish, are joined with great toil; give them my price along with the sale of the fish."
[Nahusha said:] "Let a thousand be given as the price to the Nishadas, priest, as the descendant of Bhrigu says, for the blessed one's ransom."
[Chyavana said:] "I am not worth a thousand; or what do you think, king? Let a suitable price be given; decide by your own mind."
[Nahusha said:] "Let a hundred thousand be quickly given to the Nishadas; if this should be the price, or what else do you think, blessed one?"
[Chyavana said:] "I am not to be measured by a hundred thousand, best of kings; let a suitable price be given; think with your ministers."
[Nahusha said:] "Let half the kingdom or all be given to the Nishadas; I think this is the price, or what else do you think, twice-born?"
[Chyavana said:] "I am not worth half the kingdom or all, king; let a suitable price be given; let it be thought of with sages."
[Bhishma said:] Hearing the great sage's word, Nahusha, tormented with sorrow, thought with his ministers and priest.
There another sage, a forest-dweller living on roots and fruits, born in a cow, was near Nahusha.
Addressing the king, that best of the twice-born said: "I shall please the brahmana so that he will be pleased.
I do not speak falsely, even in jest, still less otherwise; what I tell you, you should do without hesitation."
[Nahusha said:] "Let the blessed one say the price suitable for the great sage Bhrigu; save me and my country and my family from this.
The angry blessed one could burn even the three worlds entire; how much more me, lacking austerity and relying on strength of arm?
For me sunk in unfathomable water with my ministers and priests, be a raft, great sage, and decide the price."
[Bhishma said:] Hearing Nahusha's word, the mighty one born in a cow, gladdening all the ministers and the king, said:
Brahmanas, great king, are priceless, the greatest of classes, and cows, lord of the earth; let a cow be set as the price.
Hearing the great sage's word, king, Nahusha, joined with great joy, with his ministers and priest,
approached Bhrigu's son Chyavana of sharp vows and spoke this, king, as if satisfying him with his words:
Rise, rise, brahmana sage; you are bought by a cow, Bhargava; I take this as your price, best of upholders of dharma.
[Chyavana said:] "I rise, king of kings; I am rightly bought by you, sinless one; I see no wealth here equal to cows, unfallen one.
Naming, hearing, giving and seeing cows, hero, is praised, removing all sin, auspicious.
Cows are always the root of prosperity; in cows there is no sin; cows are always food, and the highest offering of the gods.
Svaha and vashat are always established in cows; cows are the leaders of sacrifice and its mouth.
They flow and bear nectar, imperishable, divine; they are the abode of nectar, saluted by all worlds.
By splendour and by form cows are like fire on earth; cows are great splendour and give happiness to beings.
The place where a herd of cows is settled and breathes fearless, it makes that place shine and removes sin.
Cows are the ladder to heaven; cows are worshipped even in heaven; cows are wish-granting goddesses; nothing else is remembered as higher.
Thus I have told the greatness of cows, best of kings; a single aspect of their qualities has been told, but a full recital cannot be."
[The Nishadas said:] "Sight and talk, sage, have been done with us; the good have seven steps for friendship; show us favour, lord.
As fire enjoys all offerings, so you, righteous-souled one, are the person-fire of great power.
We propitiate you, learned one; we bow to you; for our sake let this cow be accepted."
[Chyavana said:] "What is the eye of a wretch and of a poisonous sage burns a man to the root, like blazing fire a dry grove.
I accept the cow from you, fishermen; your sins are freed; go quickly to heaven with the fish taken in the net."
[Bhishma said:] Then by the grace of that great sage of purified self, the Nishadas went to heaven with the fish at his word.
Then King Nahusha, astonished and steady, saw the fish and the Nishadas ascending to heaven, bull of the Bharatas.
Then the one born in a cow and Chyavana, descendant of Bhrigu, offered the king fitting boons.
Then the mighty king Nahusha, lord of the earth, pleased, said "Enough," best of the Bharatas.
Then the king, like Indra, took steadiness in dharma; urged "So be it," pleased, he honoured the two sages.
His vow complete, Chyavana then went to his own hermitage, and the greatly radiant one born in a cow went to his own hermitage.
The Nishadas and the fish went to heaven, lord of men, and Nahusha, having gained a boon, entered his own city.
This has been told to you, dear one, which you asked me: what affection in sight, and what in living together, Yudhishthira.
The greatness of cows and the determination of dharma: what more shall be told, hero? What do you wish to say in your heart?
[Yudhishthira said:] My curiosity is very great about Jamadagni's son, lord: Rama, best of upholders of dharma; you ought to tell me.
How was Rama of true valour born, and how did one of kshatriya dharma come to be in a Brahmarishi's line?
Then tell fully his birth, king; and how a brahmana came from the Kaushika line, from a kshatriya.
Ah, great was the power of those two great souls, Rama and Vishvamitra, tiger among men.
How did this fault come to be, passing over the sons to their grandsons, leaving sons? You ought to tell me.
[Bhishma said:] On this too they recite this ancient Itihasa, the conversation of Chyavana and Kushika, Bharata.
Long ago, seeing this fault coming in his own line, Chyavana Bhargava, wise, best of sages,
considering all in mind, the strengths and weaknesses of qualities and faults, wishing to burn the whole line of the Kushikas, the ascetic...
The door of dharma that has been passed, ascetic, I shall make good; you ought to permit it.
[Bhishma said:] Then Kushika, with his wife, took a seat and came to where the great sage Chyavana was.
Taking up a pitcher, the king offered him foot-water and had all rites done for that great soul.
Then the king, great-souled and firm in vows, unperturbed, had him accept the honey-offering by rule.
Having honoured the brahmana, he said these words: "Blessed one, we two are dependent; say, what shall we do?
If kingdom, if wealth, if cows, sharp-vowed one, and sacrifices and gifts: say, I shall give you all.
This house, this kingdom and this seat of dharma are yours; you are king, rule the earth; I am a servant dependent on you."
When this was said, Chyavana Bhargava then replied to Kushika with great joy:

I do not want the kingdom, king, nor wealth, nor women, nor cows, nor countries, nor sacrifices; hear this.
mahabharata:13:52.21	I shall undertake a certain rule, if it pleases you two; I am to be served by you two without hesitation.
Thus addressed by him, the couple rejoiced and replied to that sage, "So be it," Bharata.
Then Kushika, glad, brought him into the best part of the house and showed him a pleasant place.
This is the blessed one's bed; stay here as you wish; we shall strive to bring you joy, ascetic.
As they spoke thus, the sun passed; then the sage asked for drink and food.
Then King Kushika, bowing, asked him, "What food is desired by you? What shall I set before you?"
Then he replied to the lord of men with great joy, "Give me suitable food that is at hand," Bharata.
Honouring his word, the king said "So be it" and gave him food as available.
Then the blessed one, having eaten, knower of dharma, said to the couple, "I wish to sleep; sleep afflicts me, lord."
Then reaching the bedroom, the blessed best of sages lay down, and the king stood with his wife.
Then Bhargava said: "I am not to be woken as I sleep; you two must massage my feet and stay awake through the night."
Kushika, without hesitation, knowing dharma, said "So be it"; and they did not wake him at the end of the night.
According to the great sage's instructions, the couple became supremely devoted to his service, restrained.
Then the blessed brahmana, having instructed the king, slept on one side for twenty-one days.
The king, fasting with his wife, descendant of the Kurus, attended him, glad, devoted to Chyavana's service.
Then the ascetic Bhargava rose himself and, saying nothing, the great ascetic left the house.
The two, best of sages in the couple, hungry and worn with toil, followed him, but he did not look at them.
King, a righteous son of Angiras named Samvarta wanders all directions, clad in the quarters, bewildering the people.
And Gandhari, greatly fortunate, wise and knowing compassion, bears grief for her sons with great steadiness, great king.
Seeing them, Arjuna the Kaurava, his eyes covered with tears, could not look at them, bereft of Krishna and of sons.
Then King Yudhishthira suddenly wished to ask her, and the blessed Indra, king of gods, told him.
